title: Ang 849–855: Bilaval ki Var
tomorrow: why would Kabir call himself crazy, and sound glad about it?

segments.voice: Last week closed on the days: every weekday pointing back to the One. This week opens with a ballad, and a question about singing.

The truck has been quiet for an hour. Dark fields, the dashboard glow, the hum of the road. Then the driver, a dad who never sings, starts on a shabad. Off-key. Half the words missing. His daughter in the passenger seat doesn't know whether to laugh or cry. Does that count as singing gurbani? The ballad of raga Bilaval opens with a salok that answers exactly that.
screen: `AN HOUR OF QUIET.` → `A DAD WHO NEVER SINGS.` → `DOES THAT COUNT?`

segments.voice: Bilaval ki Var is Guru Ram Das's ballad: pauris, his stanzas, with saloks before them. Its first salok is Guru Amar Das's. In paraphrase: sing Bilaval only when the Name is in your mouth. Then raga and sound become beautiful through the Word, when the mind settles into sahaj, a natural meditation. Then a line that surprises people. In paraphrase: set raga and sound aside and serve the Lord, and you'll be honored in his court. Nanak, the one who faces the Guru reflects on God, and the mind's pride falls away. So the measure of the song isn't the voice. It's the Name in it, and a mind that isn't showing off. That's not a dismissal of music; this is a ballad set in a raga, made to be sung, and sung well. The warning is about pride, the singer listening to himself. Here's the thing to tell a friend: the Granth's own ballad of Bilaval begins by telling you when Bilaval is worth singing. Now back to the truck. A dad, half the words gone, putting the Name in his mouth on an empty road at night, with nobody to impress. By the salok's own measure, that's Bilaval.
screen: `A BALLAD BY THE FOURTH GURU.` · `SING IT WITH THE NAME IN IT.` · `SET THE MUSIC ASIDE, AND SERVE.` · `OFF-KEY ON THE HIGHWAY.` · then, large: `THE BALLAD.`

segments.voice: If you have kirtan nearby, play a little of it quietly; if not, listen to your own breathing. Either way, for the sit, listen for what's underneath the music rather than the music itself. If you'd like, read ang 850 first.
Ang 849. Where Bilaval ki Var begins, Guru Ram Das's ballad, opened by Guru Amar Das's salok on when to sing.
The ballad: the Name in your mouth matters more than the pitch. Off-key still counts.

howItsDone: Ragis sing Bilaval ki Var salok by salok and pauri by pauri; its opening salok, by Guru Amar Das, is often cited when Sikhs talk about the spirit in which kirtan is sung.
